lesson.title: The tiny building blocks of life
points: All living things are made of cells, the basic units of life.
Robert Hooke first saw cells in a slice of cork in 1665. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.
Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. Plant cells also have a cell wall, plastids (like chloroplasts) and a large vacuole.
Cells with no well-defined nucleus, such as bacteria, are prokaryotic. Cells with a nucleus are eukaryotic.
lesson.story: Think of a cell as a small kirana shop. The shutter and door (cell membrane) decide what comes in and goes out, the floor and shelves (cytoplasm) hold everything, and the owner (nucleus) controls all the work.

example.q: A student peels a thin layer from an onion, stains it with safranin and sees box-like cells with a clear, thick outer boundary. Is it a plant cell or an animal cell?
steps: Notice the thick boundary outside the cell membrane. This is the cell wall.
Only plant cells have a cell wall. Animal cells have just a thin cell membrane.
So the onion peel cells are plant cells.

lesson.title: Growing up and making new life
points: Reproduction is asexual (one parent, as in budding of Hydra and binary fission of Amoeba) or sexual (male and female gametes fuse).
Fusion of a sperm and an egg is fertilisation and gives a zygote. It is internal in humans and external, in water, in frogs.
The zygote becomes an embryo and then a foetus. Animals that lay eggs are oviparous. Those that give birth to young ones are viviparous.
Adolescence (about 11 to 19 years) brings puberty, controlled by hormones. Whether the sperm carries X or Y decides the baby's sex.
lesson.story: A zygote is like one grain of rice sown in a paddy field. It is just one cell, but in the right place (the uterus) it divides again and again until a whole baby grows.

example.q: A female frog lays eggs in a pond and a male frog releases sperms over them. Name the type of fertilisation and say what happens next.
steps: The sperms meet the eggs outside the female's body, in water, so fertilisation is external.
The zygote develops inside the jelly-coated egg and a tadpole hatches.
The tadpole changes into an adult frog by metamorphosis.

lesson.title: Push, pull and press
points: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). Forces in the same direction add up; forces in opposite directions subtract.
Pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A. Its unit is the pascal (Pa), and 1 Pa = 1 N/m². The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure.
Liquids and gases also exert pressure. The pressure of a liquid increases with depth.
Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact. Rolling friction is less than sliding friction, and lubricants reduce friction.
lesson.story: A sharp knife cuts a tomato easily because your whole push falls on a very thin edge. A blunt knife spreads the same push over a larger area, so it hardly cuts.

example.q: A force of 500 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². Find the pressure.
steps: Pressure = force ÷ area.
So the pressure is 2000 Pa.

lesson.title: Vibrations you can hear
points: Sound is produced by vibrating objects. It needs a medium such as air, water or a solid, and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Time period = 1 ÷ frequency. Higher frequency means a higher pitch (shriller sound).
Amplitude decides loudness, which is measured in decibels (dB). A larger amplitude gives a louder sound.
Humans can hear frequencies from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Unpleasant sound is noise, and too much of it is noise pollution.
lesson.story: When a dholak is beaten, its skin vibrates and you hear the beat. Press your hand on the skin to stop the vibration and the sound stops at once.

example.q: A pendulum completes 40 oscillations in 20 seconds. Find its frequency and time period.
steps: Frequency = oscillations per second = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 Hz.
Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 s.
Check: 2 oscillations each second, each taking half a second.

lesson.title: Shiny metals and fossil fuels
points: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors.
Metal oxides are basic, while non-metal oxides are acidic. Reactive metals such as sodium react quickly with air and water, so sodium is stored in kerosene.
Metals like zinc and magnesium react with dilute acids and release hydrogen gas. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels, formed over millions of years from dead plants and animals. They are exhaustible natural resources.
lesson.story: A brass lota rings when you tap it and a steel tava carries heat from the flame to the roti. A piece of chalk, a non-metal-like material, just crumbles when you hit it. The ringing and the heat flow are the signs of a metal.

example.q: A rod is shiny, gives a ringing sound when struck, and the bulb in a circuit glows when the rod is joined in it. Is it a metal or a non-metal?
steps: Shiny surface means lustre, a property of metals.
A ringing sound when struck means it is sonorous, again a property of metals.
The bulb glows, so the rod conducts electricity. All three properties show that the rod is a metal.

lesson.title: How things burn
points: Combustion is the burning of a substance in air (oxygen) to give heat and often light. Burning needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat to reach the ignition temperature.
The ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. Substances with a very low ignition temperature, like petrol and LPG, are highly inflammable.
A candle flame has three zones: the dark inner zone, the middle luminous zone (partial combustion) and the outer non-luminous zone, which is the hottest (complete combustion).
The calorific value of a fuel is the heat in kJ produced by the complete burning of 1 kg of it. Fire is put out by cutting off the air, removing the fuel or cooling below the ignition temperature.
lesson.story: On a chulha, the firewood needs a small flame or a matchstick to start burning, but then it keeps burning on its own. The match heats the wood up to its ignition temperature, and the air supplies oxygen.

example.q: A fuel has a calorific value of 45,000 kJ/kg. How much heat is produced by completely burning 2 kg of it?
steps: Calorific value is the heat from burning 1 kg of the fuel.
Heat from 2 kg = 2 × 45,000 kJ.
So the heat produced is 90,000 kJ.

lesson.title: Bouncing light and the eye
points: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both are measured from the normal, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
A smooth surface gives regular reflection. A rough surface gives diffuse reflection, which is how we see a page from any side.

White light splits into seven colours (VIBGYOR) by dispersion, as in a rainbow. Light enters the eye through the cornea and pupil, the iris controls the size of the pupil, and the lens focuses the image on the retina.
The retina has rods for dim light and cones for bright light and colour. An image stays on the retina for about 1/16 of a second, which is persistence of vision.
lesson.story: A rubber ball thrown at a wall bounces away at the same slant it came in. A mirror does the same to a ray of light.

example.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 40°. Find the angle of reflection and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
steps: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is 40°.
Both angles are measured from the normal, on either side of it.
Angle between the two rays = 40° + 40° = 80°.
